title: 9 warning signs of identity theft you should never ignore
summary: Nine identity theft warning signs range from unfamiliar credit inquiries to SIM swap attacks that can quietly drain your bank account funds.
story: Cybercrime losses reached nearly $21 billion last year, prompting Kurt Knutsson to warn of increasingly sophisticated AI scams. He joins 'Fox & Friends Weekend' to break down the FBI data, highlighting that investment fraud alone cost victims $8.65 billion. Knutsson hosts a free live class to teach families how to protect their money and secure accounts.

Identity theft can start quietly. You may not see a drained bank account or a maxed-out credit card. The first warning could be a strange letter in the mail, an unfamiliar inquiry on your credit report or a password reset alert you never requested.

Those little clues are easy to brush off, but catching them early can give you more time to protect your money, credit and accounts. One unusual message does not automatically mean someone has stolen your identity, so do not panic. Instead, verify what happened and pay attention to anything else that looks out of place.
Here are nine identity theft warning signs you should never ignore.
CYBERCRIME LOSSES NEAR $21B: 5 WAYS TO PROTECT YOUR MONEY
Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the Protect Your Money replay
Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, Protect Your Money From Today’s Biggest Threats, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay and download our financial protection checklist.

Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five simple ways to help defend yourself against AI scams, fraud, identity theft and financial hacks. You’ll learn how to set up bank alerts, strengthen your account logins, protect your phone number, freeze your credit and help secure your retirement savings against unauthorized transfers. No technical experience is needed.
Get the free replay and checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com

Identity theft can begin with subtle warning signs, including unfamiliar credit inquiries, password reset alerts, strange bills or unexpected account changes. (Ute Grabowsky/Photothek via Getty Images)
1) You receive a data breach notice
A company may contact you after discovering that customer information was exposed. The notice could come from a bank, retailer, employer, healthcare provider, insurer, school or another organization.

Read it carefully. Find out what information may have been involved, when the incident occurred and whether the company is offering steps such as password changes or credit monitoring. Save the notice with your other records.
A breach notice shows possible exposure, not confirmed identity theft. Still, it is a good reason to review your accounts and strengthen your security.
2) An unfamiliar credit inquiry appears
Check your credit reports for hard inquiries you do not recognize. A hard inquiry generally appears when a lender reviews your credit after you apply for credit.

Also look for new accounts, unfamiliar addresses, collections accounts or loans you never requested. Identity thieves may use stolen information to apply for credit before you notice anything unusual.
Check all three major credit bureaus rather than relying on a single report. Details can differ from one report to another, so reviewing only one may leave gaps.
If you find an inquiry or account that does not belong to you, contact the lender using a trusted phone number or website rather than contact information from a suspicious message.
3) You get bills or collection calls for accounts you never opened

A bill for a credit card, utility service, medical account or buy-now-pay-later purchase you did not make is a serious warning sign. So is a call from a debt collector about a debt that does not belong to you.
Do not ignore the notice simply because you believe it is a mistake. Ask the organization for details, dispute the account and keep copies of your correspondence.
Be cautious about sharing personal information with an unexpected caller. If you need to contact a company, find its official number independently.
4) Your bank, card or payment app shows unfamiliar activity

Review checking, savings, credit card, payment app, investment and retirement accounts regularly. Look for small test charges, unfamiliar withdrawals, new payees, password changes, profile updates or transfers you did not authorize.
Scammers sometimes begin with a small transaction to see whether an account is active. Other times, they try to take over the account entirely.

Contact the financial institution immediately through its official app, website or statement. Ask what steps are needed to secure the account, replace cards, investigate transactions and protect any linked accounts.
Turn on account alerts for purchases, transfers, password changes and other important activity. Alerts are useful, but they work best when you still review statements yourself.
5) A government notice does not match your activity

Pay attention to unexpected letters or online notices from the IRS, Social Security Administration or a state agency. Examples include a tax return you did not file, benefits you did not request or a claim connected to an employer you do not recognize.
Do not respond using a link or phone number in an unsolicited message. Visit the agency's official website or use a phone number from a statement or a previously verified account.
Keep every notice. Government-related identity theft can take time to resolve, and a clear record of dates and communications may help.
6) Your phone suddenly stops working or your number changes

A phone that unexpectedly loses service can have an innocent explanation, such as an outage or billing problem. But it can also be a sign that someone transferred your number to another device or took over your mobile account.

That is exactly what happened to Patricia Escriva, whose phone suddenly lost service before scammers used a SIM swap attack to get into her accounts and steal thousands of dollars. We broke down her story and what you can learn from it in The CyberGuy Report podcast: How hackers drain your bank account in minutes.

If your phone suddenly goes offline, and you cannot explain why, treat it as a warning sign. Contact your wireless provider right away from another phone and ask whether there was a recent SIM change, number transfer or account update. A SIM is the small card or digital profile that connects your phone to a mobile network.
Once your number is secure, review important accounts for password resets or login attempts. Ask your carrier about an account PIN or other protections against unauthorized changes.
HEALTHCARE DATA BREACH EXPOSES 3.75M PATIENT RECORDS

Unexpected bank activity, collection calls or government notices may signal identity theft and should be verified promptly through trusted channels. (Isabelle Souriment/Hans Lucas/AFP via Getty Images)
7) You receive password reset or login alerts you did not request

An unexpected password reset email, multifactor authentication code or sign-in alert may mean that someone is trying to access an account. It may also be a fake message designed to trick you into clicking a link.

Do not share a verification code with anyone who calls or messages you. Open the account through its official app or type the website address yourself, then review recent activity and change the password if needed.

Start with your primary email account. Email often acts as the doorway to password resets for banking, shopping, healthcare and other services. Use a long, unique password and turn on multifactor authentication, which requires an extra verification step beyond your password.
Avoid reusing passwords. If one website is breached, a reused password may give criminals an opportunity to try the same combination elsewhere.
8) Your personal details suddenly appear in unusually convincing scams

A sudden wave of calls, texts or emails that use your correct name, address, family details or account information deserves attention. This does not prove identity theft, but it may indicate that personal data is circulating among scammers.

Be especially cautious when a message creates urgency, demands payment, asks for a verification code or tells you to move money to "protect" it. Banks, government agencies and legitimate companies do not need you to hand over a one-time code to keep your account safe.
Instead of replying, contact the organization through a trusted channel. Then review your accounts, credit reports and recent security alerts.
9) Your address, account profile or identity information changes without permission

An unfamiliar mailing address on a credit report, a changed email address on an account or a notification that your identity was verified somewhere you do not recognize can signal an attempted takeover.
Review account recovery information, authorized users, linked devices and connected apps. Remove anything you do not recognize and change the password from a trusted device.

If the change involves a bank, credit card, phone provider or government account, contact that organization promptly. A small profile change can be an early step in a larger attempt to control the account.
What to do if you spot one of these signs
First, slow down and verify the information. A suspicious text may be a scam, and a legitimate account alert may be the result of a family member's purchase or a forgotten subscription.
If the activity is confirmed, or you cannot explain it, take these important steps:
Use a trusted number or official app. Ask the organization to secure the account and investigate.

A credit freeze restricts access to your credit file, making it harder for someone to open new credit in your name. Place a freeze with all three major credit bureaus if appropriate for your situation.
A fraud alert asks lenders to take extra steps to verify your identity. It provides another layer of protection and works differently from a credit freeze.
Change important passwords, use a password manager to create and store strong, unique passwords, review recovery settings and add account protections through your wireless provider.
Check banking, credit cards, payment apps, investments, retirement, healthcare, utilities and government services.
Save breach notices, screenshots, dates, names, dispute numbers and copies of letters.

If you confirm that someone has used your identity, report it to the Federal Trade Commission at IdentityTheft.gov. The site will help you create an FTC Identity Theft Report and build a personalized recovery plan. You can also use that report when working with credit bureaus, businesses and debt collectors to dispute fraudulent accounts or information. Some companies may also ask for a police report.

If your information appears in a breach, you may not be able to remove it completely. Focus on making the exposed information less useful. Freeze your credit, secure your accounts, limit unnecessary public information and keep watching for new warning signs.
Where identity theft monitoring services fit

You can take many important steps to protect yourself, including checking your accounts, using unique passwords and freezing your credit. An identity theft monitoring service can add another layer by watching for signs that your personal or financial information may be misused.

Depending on the service and plan you choose, monitoring can include credit reports, checking and savings accounts, investments and 401(k) accounts, bank account takeovers, home title changes, phone takeovers, identity verification, dark web exposure, data breaches and social media activity.

That broader monitoring can be helpful because identity theft can show up in more places than your credit report. If fraud occurs, restoration support may also help reduce the burden of dealing with calls, paperwork and disputes.

Monitoring works best as an added layer of protection rather than a replacement for good security habits. Continue reviewing your accounts, watching for unusual activity and acting quickly when something looks wrong. See my tips and best picks on Best Identity Theft Protection at Cyberguy.com
NEW BANK SCAM LAWS COULD STOP SUSPICIOUS PAYMENTS
A phone that suddenly loses service could signal a SIM swap, potentially giving criminals access to accounts tied to the victim’s phone number. (Celine Frohnapfel/picture alliance via Getty Images)
Kurt's key takeaways

Identity theft often gives you warning signs before serious damage is done. A strange charge, an account you do not recognize or even a password reset alert you never requested can be your cue to take a closer look. Trust your gut when something feels off, verify what happened and act quickly to lock down your accounts and credit.

A few minutes spent checking now could save you a much bigger headache later. The key is to stay alert without living in fear. Keep an eye on your accounts, use strong security protections and know what steps to take if your information ends up in the wrong hands.

title: Robot dog could deliver your next package and an ad
summary: Robot.com's R-dog uses articulated legs and wheels to climb stairs and deliver packages, while its built-in screens display paid ads along the route.
story: Smart refrigerators, cars and computers can show ads after updates, raising privacy and ownership concerns, Kurt ‘CyberGuy’ Knutsson explains.

We've covered robot dogs patrolling with police and training to handle terrain that could someday take them to the moon. We've even watched wheeled versions tackle some pretty wild ground. And whenever we show these machines, one question keeps coming up: What happens when they reach a flight of stairs? Well, Robot.com may have an answer.

Its new four-legged R-dog is built to carry packages where traditional wheeled delivery robots can get stuck. It can also show ads along the way, turning your future delivery into something of a moving billboard.
So, can R-dog really get your package closer to your front door while making the economics of robot delivery work? Let's take a closer look.
ONE-WHEELED AI SECURITY ROBOT COULD PATROL YOUR PROPERTY
Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the Protect Your Money replay
Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, Protect Your Money From Today’s Biggest Threats, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay and download our financial protection checklist.

Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five simple ways to help defend yourself against AI scams, fraud, identity theft and financial hacks. You’ll learn how to set up bank alerts, strengthen your account logins, protect your phone number, freeze your credit and help secure your retirement savings against unauthorized transfers. No technical experience is needed.
Get the free replay and checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com
R-dog combines wheels, articulated legs and artificial intelligence to tackle the difficult final stretch of package delivery. (robot.com)
What is the R-dog robot dog?

R-dog is Robot.com's latest concept for autonomous delivery. The San Francisco-based company unveiled it on Aug. 11. The idea tackles one of the most frustrating parts of robotic delivery: the final stretch to your door. A wheeled robot may handle the sidewalk just fine, only to meet a curb or staircase it cannot cross. Robot.com designed R-dog to cover those final 330 feet with a mix of wheels and articulated legs.

Each leg ends in a wheel, so R-dog can roll efficiently across flatter ground. When the route gets more difficult, those flexible legs are designed to help it deal with stairs, curbs and other obstacles. The cargo compartment forms most of the robot's body. Robot.com says it can carry food orders and standard packages inside.

And yes, it definitely looks like a robot dog. There is even a tail, which gives the machine a friendlier appearance than your average delivery box on wheels. That personality may be more than decoration. Robot.com wants people to notice R-dog, interact with it and feel comfortable when it appears in public spaces. As you will see, that becomes especially important once advertising enters the picture.
Why stairs are such a headache for delivery robots

Getting a delivery robot across town can actually be easier than getting it from the sidewalk to your front door. Traditional delivery robots tend to perform best on predictable surfaces. Smooth sidewalks work well because wheels are efficient and relatively simple.

Then the terrain changes. A staircase can end the trip. A high curb can cause trouble. Even an awkward building entrance may force someone to step in. That creates an obvious weak point in a system that is supposed to reduce human involvement. Robot.com wants R-dog to keep going when a standard sidewalk robot would have to stop.

Its four-legged design could also expand the places where autonomous delivery makes sense. Campuses, apartment complexes and neighborhoods can all include routes that become difficult for wheels alone. Of course, getting over the obstacle is only useful if the package also reaches the right person. That brings us to R-dog's unusual delivery system.
How R-dog drops off your package

The cargo compartment can hold multiple items, including stacked food orders and e-commerce packages. Once R-dog reaches its destination, an unattended auto drop-off system releases the order. The robot can then continue to its next assignment. And yes, the visual is hard to ignore.

The package appears to slide out through the back of the robot. There really is no delicate way to say this: It looks a little like R-dog poops out your delivery. Funny visual aside, the system could have a practical advantage. You would not necessarily need to stand outside and physically unload the robot before it could leave.

Still, one question remains. Robot.com says the compartment can carry multiple orders, but its current materials do not explain exactly how the concept chooses the correct package when several items are loaded inside. That is one of the details I want to see explained as R-dog gets closer to real-world deployment. The company is still refining parts of the prototype, including its storage setup.
HUMANOID ROBOTS WORK NONSTOP IN PACKAGE TEST
Robot.com’s R-dog uses wheeled legs to climb stairs, carry packages and display advertising during autonomous deliveries. (robot.com)
Why R-dog also shows ads

Now we get to the part that makes R-dog more than a quirky delivery machine. The robot has two video screens connected to R-ads, Robot.com's advertising platform. Brands can remotely manage campaigns shown on the company's robots.

In other words, every trip can potentially earn money twice. The robot can perform a delivery while its screens carry paid advertising through the neighborhood. That business model makes some sense. People already ignore plenty of static advertising. A four-legged robot rolling past with a tail has a much better chance of making someone look.

You might stop to watch it. Maybe you pull out your phone for a photo or video. Someone else could share that clip on social media. From an advertiser's perspective, that kind of attention can be valuable. Robot.com also promotes natural voice conversations, allowing R-dog to respond when people interact with it. That could make the advertising experience more engaging than simply walking past another screen.

The company says R-ads also offer campaign analytics. However, its public R-dog materials leave some details about those measurements unclear. I would like to know exactly what the system measures when people interact with these robots and how that information gets handled. Those answers become more important if machines like R-dog eventually appear in busy public spaces.
How AI helps R-dog find its way

Of course, legs alone do not get a robot safely through a crowded neighborhood. It also needs to understand what is happening around it. Robot.com is working with FieldAI on the navigation stack planned for the production version of R-dog.

FieldAI's Field Foundation Models are designed to help robots operate in changing real-world environments without requiring prior mapping. That could allow R-dog to adapt when the route ahead looks different from what it expected, whether someone left an object in the way or the path suddenly changes.

Robot.com also runs its fleet through a platform called REMI. The company describes REMI as its fleet-management platform and physical API layer. The advantage here is that R-dog does not need an entirely separate operational system. Robot.com can plug the new four-legged design into technology it already uses across its fleet.
CEO and co-founder Felipe Chavez Cortes summed up that strategy when he said, "We built R-dog to run on what already exists."
Robot.com already has robots in the real world

R-dog may be new, but Robot.com has already spent years putting robots to work. The company was founded in 2017 and is headquartered in San Francisco, with additional offices in Colombia. Robot.com says more than 500 robots are deployed across the United States and Canada, plus Dubai and other MENA markets. Those machines have completed more than 2.5 million tasks.

Its lineup includes R-kiwi for sidewalk delivery and R-cargo for industrial logistics. Robot.com also develops R-noid, a humanoid platform aimed at workplace tasks. That existing fleet gives Robot.com experience to build on.
When and where will R-dog launch?

Robot.com says commercial deployments are targeted for 2027. The company's CEO has said college campuses will come first, although Robot.com has yet to announce specific campuses or cities. That makes campuses a logical proving ground. They offer lots of short deliveries, plenty of foot traffic and exactly the kinds of curbs or stairways that R-dog was designed to handle.
Robot.com already operates campus delivery robots in North America and expanded its autonomous delivery partnership with Sodexo in August 2026.

Pricing has not been announced. And do not expect to walk into a store and buy an R-dog for your house. At least initially, Robot.com appears focused on commercial delivery pilots and brand activations rather than individual consumers.
For now, businesses can sign up for early access to delivery pilots and advertising activations ahead of the planned 2027 rollout.
NEW WHEELED ROBOT SAYS NO THANKS TO HUMANOID HYPE
Robot.com plans to pair autonomous delivery with mobile advertising through two video screens built into its R-dog robot. (robot.com)
What this means to you

If R-dog performs the way Robot.com hopes, robot delivery could get closer to your actual doorstep instead of stopping at the sidewalk. That could make autonomous delivery practical in more places and reduce the number of times a person has to step in to finish the trip.

But R-dog also gives us a preview of where the economics of robot delivery may be heading. Moving a package is one revenue opportunity. Selling advertising during the journey creates another. That means your future delivery experience could look very different. The same machine bringing dinner to your door might also be displaying a commercial as it rolls away.

Convenience will get plenty of attention, but I will also be watching the privacy side. Robot.com should be clear about what its advertising system measures when people approach or interact with R-dog.
Kurt's key takeaways

I have seen plenty of robot dogs that can climb, jump or show off in a demo. R-dog caught my attention because Robot.com is trying to apply those abilities to a very ordinary problem: getting a package all the way to your door. Wheels are great until the sidewalk ends.

Giving a delivery robot articulated legs could help it complete routes that stop other machines short. The advertising angle may be equally important to whether this idea works as a business. If R-dog can earn money from an ad while it is already out making a delivery, that gives operators another reason to deploy it.

Still, R-dog remains a concept heading toward commercial use in 2027. I want to see how it handles real stairs, crowded sidewalks and everyday weather before calling the problem solved. I also want more details about how multiple packages get sorted during unattended deliveries and what information R-ads collect from public interactions. Those answers will tell us a lot about whether R-dog becomes a useful delivery tool or simply a very clever way to get people to look at a screen.

Would you be comfortable with a robot dog climbing your steps to deliver a package if it was also showing ads along the way, or would you rather stick with a human at the door? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.

title: Fake patient portal scam can steal your login and infect your PC
summary: MyChart phishing emails mimic real patient portal alerts with fake lab results and malware tricks that target Windows users across the country.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

If you have ever checked a lab result or sent your doctor a message online, you may already know MyChart. It is a widely used patient portal from Epic that hospitals and medical practices use to give patients online access to health information and care teams.

That growing reliance on patient portals caught the attention of Mary M. She recently wrote to us after hearing from her primary care physician, or PCP, and several specialists about moving more of their patient communication online.
"I just got a lot of updates from my PCP and specialist doctors saying they are moving toward this, but they are already compromised!! I think this is a topic for you!"

Mary raised a concern many patients may share as they hear about scams targeting MyChart users. There is an important point to clear up. The warnings reviewed here describe criminals impersonating MyChart through phishing campaigns. They do not report a breach of the MyChart platform itself.
MEDICARE AND SOCIAL SECURITY SCAMS: WARNING SIGNS AND TIPS
MyChart phishing scams use fake medical results and bogus Medicare offers to exploit trust in patient portals and push victims into sharing sensitive information. (Epic Systems Corporation)

Epic has documented scams that copy the MyChart experience to steal login details. One version can also push malware onto Windows computers. Here's how the scam works and how to protect yourself before a fake MyChart alert catches you off guard.

You’ll learn how to set up bank alerts, strengthen your account logins, protect your phone number, freeze your credit and help secure your retirement savings against unauthorized transfers. No technical experience is needed.

Why the MyChart phishing scam is getting attention now

This one caught my attention because the warnings are coming from several credible sources at nearly the same time. Penn Medicine said on Aug. 26, 2026, that it was seeing a nationwide scam involving emails and text messages made to look like they came from MyChart. Then, on Aug. 28, Pennsylvania Attorney General Dave Sunday warned consumers about another MyChart impersonation scam involving a bogus Medicare Kit.

Epic has also detailed two phishing campaigns its security team investigated this summer. Put all of that together, and you can see why I want you to be especially careful with unexpected MyChart messages right now.

The tricky part is that many of us are already used to getting legitimate emails about appointments or new test results. A fake MyChart alert can land right alongside the real ones, and scammers are counting on you reacting before you take a closer look.
How the fake MyChart results scam works
One campaign starts with a message that looks routine. Epic says the email carries MyChart branding and tells the recipient, "Your recent results are ready."
The button inside the email leads to a fake sign-in page. According to Epic, scammers copied code from the real MyChart site, which helps the page look convincing.
The bogus page asks for an email address and password. If you enter them, the scammers can capture those credentials. Then the attack gets more aggressive.
Fake medical results create panic
After the victim signs in, the fake site displays a made-up medical record. Epic says one version shows a pop-up claiming an "AI-powered review" found critical patterns in blood work.
That is a powerful pressure tactic. A warning about your health can be much harder to ignore than an ordinary phishing message.
Epic says real critical results come from your care team rather than a website pop-up. The fake chart then claims you need to complete a human verification step before seeing more information.
The verification step can install malware

This part should stop you immediately. Epic says the site instructs Windows users to press the Windows key and R, paste content from the clipboard and press Enter. Those steps open the Windows Run box and execute a command the website placed on the clipboard. According to Epic, following those instructions installs malware.

Epic also saw an August 2026 version with an "Unlock Full Report & See Diagnosis" button. Clicking it downloaded a Windows file called Full_Analysis_Report.exe. The page then coached the victim through bypassing the computer's security warning. Your medical results should appear inside MyChart. A patient portal should never require you to download a Windows program to reveal a diagnosis.
FAKE PASSWORD-MANAGER ALERTS COULD PUT YOUR VAULT AT RISK
Fake MyChart pages can mimic real patient portals, using alarming medical claims to pressure users into entering passwords or running malicious Windows commands. (iStock)
Another scam promises a free Medicare Health Kit

The second campaign uses a different hook. Epic says scammers sent fake emails telling people they had been selected for a "2026 Medicare Health Kit." Penn Medicine has also warned about messages advertising a free "MyChart Medicare Kit" or "Senior Health Package." MyChart does not run giveaways.

After someone clicks, Epic says the link can pass through unrelated advertising sites before reaching a fake MyChart-branded survey. A countdown clock pushes the victim to move quickly. Eventually, the site says the kit costs $0 but asks for a shipping fee. Before payment, it collects personal information. The final page asks for credit card details. Epic says no kit ships.
Why a fake MyChart message can be so convincing

Patients already expect electronic messages from doctors and hospitals. A real test-result notification may show up on the same day as a fake one. Scammers can copy that familiar routine. They can also use fear to shorten the amount of time you spend checking a message.

If a fake portal hints at a serious health problem, your first instinct may be to find out what happened. That is why opening the portal independently can make such a difference. We recently covered another healthcare scam that uses fake QR codes around medical settings. Those codes can send patients to bogus sites asking for patient portal credentials or Medicare information. The MyChart campaign follows the same basic idea. The scammer borrows trust from a healthcare service you already recognize.
How to stay safe from fake MyChart messages
A few simple steps can help you slow things down before an urgent-looking message leads you to the wrong place.

If an email says a new result is waiting, avoid using the button inside the message. Open the MyChart app directly. You can also use a saved bookmark or start from your healthcare provider's official website. Epic says each healthcare organization can have its own MyChart URL. You can use MyChart.org to find your provider's official portal.

Do not rely on the sender name alone. An email can display "MyChart" while coming from an unrelated address. Look at the full address and compare it with previous legitimate messages from your healthcare provider. If anything feels off, contact your provider through a phone number or website you already trust.

MyChart says it will never tell you to use keyboard shortcuts or run a command to verify, fix or unlock your account. A website asking you to open the Windows Run box should be an immediate warning sign. Close the page.

MyChart supports two-step verification (2FA). The extra check can help protect your account if someone gets your password. Depending on your setup, you can verify your login through a code or an authenticator app. MyChart also supports passkeys, which can reduce your reliance on a reusable password.

Avoid reusing a password from another important account. A password manager can create and store a strong password for you. If a phishing site captures one password, reuse can turn one stolen login into a much larger problem.

The malware part of this scam shows why strong security protection still has a role. Strong antivirus software can help warn you about malicious downloads or suspicious websites. Keep Windows and your browser updated too. For more ways to recognize suspicious email, see our guide on how to spot and prevent phishing attacks in your inbox.

If a message claims a serious result needs immediate attention, do not let the urgency decide what you click. Open the official MyChart app yourself or call your provider using a number you already trust. Epic specifically warns that real critical results come from your care team rather than a scary website pop-up.

Scammers can make phishing messages more convincing when they already know details such as your phone number, home address, age or family connections. A data removal service can help remove some of that information from people-search sites and data brokers. It will not stop a fake MyChart message from reaching you, but it can give scammers less personal information to work with when they try to make a message feel legitimate. Check out my top picks for data removal services and get a free scan to find out if your personal information is already out on the web by visiting CyberGuy.com.
Epic says MyChart does not run giveaways. If an email promises a free Medicare kit or health package under the MyChart name, do not enter personal information or payment details.
FAKE PARTY INVITATION SCAM CAN HIJACK YOUR COMPUTER
Patients should open MyChart directly through the official app or their healthcare provider’s website rather than clicking links in unexpected emails or texts. (iStock)
What to do if you already clicked a fake MyChart link
Your next move depends on what happened after you opened the page.

Close the page. If you did not enter any information, run a command or download a file, avoid interacting with the site any further. Mark the original message as junk or phishing. Do not click an unsubscribe link inside the suspicious message.

Go to MyChart through the official app or your provider's trusted website. Change your password right away. Then review the contact information saved in your account, including your email address and phone number. If anything looks unfamiliar, contact your healthcare organization's MyChart help desk.
Call your bank or card issuer using the number printed on the card. Tell them the card information went to a fraudulent website and ask about replacing the card.

Disconnect the computer from the internet. Have the computer checked before you use it again for sensitive activity. Run a full security scan with strong antivirus software. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android and iOS devices at CyberGuy.com. Then change important passwords from another trusted device if you used those accounts on the affected computer.

Contact your healthcare provider and health insurer. Medical identity theft can create problems beyond a stolen password. Fraudulent activity can end up connected to your health records or insurance. We explain the warning signs and recovery steps in medical identity theft follows you into the doctor's office.
Kurt's key takeaways

What gets me about this scam is how naturally it fits into something many of us already do. Doctors want patients using portals because they make it easier to see results and stay connected with a care team. Scammers know those messages already have our attention. I would keep using MyChart if my doctors rely on it. I would simply change how I respond to unexpected notifications. If an email says an important result is waiting, I would open the app myself rather than letting the email choose where I go. The malware trick also deserves extra attention. A website asking you to open the Windows Run box or ignore a security warning has crossed a very clear line. Close it and verify the message through your provider. The hardest part may be resisting the fear factor. A message about an abnormal medical result can make anyone move quickly. Taking a few extra seconds to open the real app could protect your patient account and your computer.

title: Fox News AI Newsletter: The network driving fight against data centers, Flock cameras
summary: The Fox News AI Newsletter covers the latest artificial intelligence technology advancements, including the challenges and opportunities AI presents now and for the future.
story: Rob Joyce, former cybersecurity director at the National Security Council, tells Fox News Digital the "influence actions are cognitive warfare" with unsuspecting Americans arguing "for the outcomes Beijing wants."
IN TODAY’S NEWSLETTER:
- ‘No Kings’ protest network behind fight against AI data centers and Flock cameras
- US adversary turns up the heat on America’s AI lead with an underestimated edge
- OpenAI's ChatGPT pivots after previously putting Trump alongside Putin as top threats to democracy

CROSSED WIRES: The same hard-left network behind "No Kings" and other protests is leading the battle against data centers and Flock surveillance cameras, according to a Fox News Digital investigation and a new report.

SILICON STANDOFF: China is racing to build the data centers and energy infrastructure needed to power artificial intelligence, raising concerns that Beijing’s ability to rapidly construct massive projects could help it get closer to America’s commanding lead in the physical infrastructure underpinning the AI race.

MACHINE VERDICT: OpenAI’s ChatGPT originally rated President Donald Trump as a major threat to democracy when prompted, according to a new study, but the results differed following an inquiry from Fox News Digital.

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani speaks during a press conference following a fatal stabbing incident in Times Square near West 42nd Street and Seventh Avenue in Manhattan, New York, on Aug. 31, 2026. (Kyle Mazza/Anadolu via Getty Images)
CITY HALL RIFT: New York City public school students under 9th Grade will be banned from using generative AI for at least one year, Mayor Zohran Mamdani announced Wednesday.

'SAME PLAYBOOK': As the development of data centers continues to grow into one of the top hot button political issues in the United States, some experts are sounding the alarm on the various left-wing groups and climate activists who are pouring money and resources into data center opposition campaigns.
GRID ON THE BRINK: Your lights. Your water. Your hospital. Your internet. All four depend on digital systems that foreign hackers are now targeting.
President Donald Trump delivers remarks at the "Winning the AI Race" AI Summit at the Andrew W. Mellon Auditorium in Washington, D.C., on July 23, 2025. (Getty)

‘BACKWARDS AND POOR’: President Donald Trump took aim Monday at the growing backlash against data centers, warning that communities that shut the door on the facilities risk missing out on the jobs and economic gains of America's AI boom.

OPINION: Very few people disagree. Artificial intelligence (AI) and robotics will profoundly impact the lives of every man, woman and child in our country. These revolutionary technologies will radically change our economy and, quite likely, eliminate tens of millions of jobs over the next decade.

BIG TECH BATTLE: It’s the fall of 2028. A debate moderator turns to two presidential nominees who spent their governorships fighting over data centers. "China’s AI lead is now a fact," she says. title: Android Motion Assist could ease car sickness on your phone
summary: Google's Motion Assist places animated dots on Pixel screens to combat motion sickness in vehicles, but the Android 17 rollout remains limited.
story: It’s Distracted Driver Awareness Month, and automakers like GM are putting a focus on high-tech solutions to keep drivers safe behind the wheel.
Ever tried to answer a text from the passenger seat and felt your stomach turn before you reached the second line? For people prone to motion sickness, a phone can go from useful to unbearable fast.

Google is now rolling out a great Android tool designed to make that screen easier to tolerate while the vehicle moves. It is called Motion Assist, and it places animated dots around the edges of your screen that react to the motion of the vehicle.

Apple has offered a similar feature, Vehicle Motion Cues, since iOS 18 arrived in 2024. Google began working on its own version around the same time. It originally appeared under the name Motion Cues before Google renamed it Motion Assist. Now some Pixel owners are starting to see the finished feature on phones running Android 17.
Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the Protect Your Money replay

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, Protect Your Money From Today’s Biggest Threats, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay and download our financial protection checklist. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five simple ways to help defend yourself against AI scams, fraud, identity theft and financial hacks. You’ll learn how to set up bank alerts, strengthen your account logins, protect your phone number, freeze your credit and help secure your retirement savings against unauthorized transfers. No technical experience is needed.
Get the free replay and checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com
SAMSUNG GALAXY Z FOLD8 LINEUP ADDS THREE CHOICES

Google is rolling out Motion Assist, a new Android feature that uses animated screen cues to help reduce motion sickness for passengers using their phones in moving vehicles. (NickyLloyd via Getty Images)
Why looking at your phone can make you feel sick
Your eyes may tell your brain that you are sitting still and staring at a steady screen. Meanwhile, your inner ear can feel the car moving underneath you.
Those mixed signals can trigger motion sickness. The CDC says it can happen when what you see does not match the movement your body feels, which can leave you nauseous or dizzy.
Reading a text or scrolling through your phone can make things worse because your eyes stay focused on a screen that appears still while the car keeps moving.
How Android Motion Assist works
Motion Assist gives your eyes another visual clue. Small shapes appear around the edges of the display while you continue using the app in the middle of the screen.
Your phone uses motion sensors, including its accelerometer and gyroscope, to follow changes in the vehicle. As the car turns or changes speed, the on-screen cues move along with that motion.
The goal is to give your eyes information that lines up more closely with what your body feels. That may reduce the sensory mismatch that can leave you reaching for the window button.

Google's version also gives you control over the look of the cues with options for shape, size, color and opacity. You can also have Motion Assist activate automatically when your phone detects that you are traveling in a moving vehicle.
Android Motion Assist is rolling out slowly

Here is the frustrating part. You may have Android 17 and still come up empty when you look for Motion Assist. So far, the feature has appeared on select Pixel phones running Android 17. This seems to be a staged rollout rather than a single switch flipped for everyone at once.

The feature appears to arrive through Google Play services rather than through a separate Motion Assist app. Google explains that its system services can deliver new features separately from the main Android operating system update. Google has yet to publish a dedicated Motion Assist support page or a complete list of supported Android phones. So, for now, Android 17 alone may still leave you waiting.
12 BIGGEST APPLE WWDC 2026 TAKEAWAYS YOU NEED TO KNOW
Android users may soon get a built-in way to make reading or texting in the car more comfortable with Google’s new Motion Assist feature. (Hispanolistic via Getty Images)
How to turn on Motion Assist on Android
If Motion Assist has reached your Pixel, here is where to look:

Open Settings.Tap your Google profile at the top.Tap All services.Scroll down to Personal & device safety.Tap Motion Assist.Turn on Start in a moving vehicle if you want Motion Assist to activate automatically when your phone detects that you are riding in a moving vehicle.
Open Settings.
Tap your Google profile at the top.
Tap All services.
Scroll down to Personal & device safety.
Tap Motion Assist.
Turn on Start in a moving vehicle if you want Motion Assist to activate automatically when your phone detects that you are riding in a moving vehicle.
You can also add a Motion Assist tile to Quick Settings so you can turn the feature on or off manually.
Motion Assist also lets you customize the color, shape and opacity of the on-screen cues. A Randomization option can automatically vary those settings.

If you do not see Motion Assist, that does not necessarily mean anything is wrong with your phone. Google appears to be rolling out the feature in stages, and it is still missing from some Pixel phones running Android 17.
What to do if Motion Assist is missing

If you do not see Motion Assist on your Pixel, first make sure your phone is up to date. To check for the latest Pixel software, go to Settings > System > Software updates and install any available update.
Then check your Google Play system update. Go to Settings > Security & privacy > System & updates > Google Play system update. Install any available update and restart your phone if prompted.

However, updating your Pixel may not make Motion Assist appear right away. As mentioned above, Google appears to be rolling out the feature gradually. So, if your phone is fully updated and Motion Assist remains missing, you may simply have to wait for Google to enable it on your device.
How to turn on Vehicle Motion Cues on iPhone
If you have an iPhone, Apple already offers its version of the same idea.
Here is how to turn on Vehicle Motion Cues:

Open Settings.Tap Accessibility.Tap Motion.Tap Vehicle Motion Cues.Choose Automatically in Vehicle if you want your iPhone to turn the feature on when it detects that you are riding in a moving vehicle.
Open Settings.
Tap Accessibility.
Tap Motion.
Tap Vehicle Motion Cues.
Choose Automatically in Vehicle if you want your iPhone to turn the feature on when it detects that you are riding in a moving vehicle.
You can also choose On when you want the cues displayed continuously.

Apple lets you customize the pattern and color. You can also change the size or number of dots shown around the screen. Apple says the feature works best when you are seated facing forward. One important safety note: use this as a passenger feature. Apple warns against using Vehicle Motion Cues while operating a moving vehicle.
ANDROID FAKE CALL DETECTION WARNS YOU ABOUT SCAMS
Google’s Motion Assist uses your phone’s motion sensors to display moving dots that may help reduce the sensory mismatch linked to motion sickness. (Baona via Getty Images)
Will moving dots really help motion sickness?

The idea may sound almost too simple, but it targets the sensory conflict linked to motion sickness. Still, everyone responds differently. Apple describes Vehicle Motion Cues as a feature that may help reduce motion sickness. Google uses similar language for Motion Assist.

Think of the moving cues as another tool you can try rather than a guaranteed fix. If the screen still makes you feel sick, put the phone down and look toward the horizon. The CDC includes looking at the horizon among its strategies for reducing motion sickness.
Another option is to listen instead of looking at your phone. We have a step-by-step guide showing how to get your phone to read articles aloud on both iPhone and Android at Cyberguy.com.
Why this Android feature is worth checking
A row of moving dots may sound like a tiny phone feature until you are the person who cannot answer a message from the back seat without feeling queasy.
That is what makes Motion Assist interesting. Google is trying to solve a very ordinary problem using sensors already inside your phone. You need no extra app or accessory.
If the feature works for you, a car ride could become a chance to catch up on messages or read something longer without immediately regretting it.
Kurt's key takeaways

I like phone features that solve an annoyance you feel in everyday life. Motion Assist falls squarely into that category. If you get motion sickness, I would try the automatic setting as soon as it appears on your Pixel. There is very little effort involved, and you will know quickly whether the moving cues help you. iPhone owners already have a similar option hiding in Accessibility. That is also a good reminder to explore those settings from time to time. Some of the most useful features on your phone can sit there unnoticed for months.
Would moving dots on your screen make you more willing to use your phone during a car ride, or would you rather put the phone away completely? Let us know by writing to us at Cyberguy.com

title: The privacy risk of moving to a retirement community
summary: Moving to a 55+ community can quickly expose your data to scammers and data brokers before you even unpack, putting your whole family at risk.
story: Artificial intelligence is rapidly accelerating elder fraud schemes across the U.S., targeting older Americans who hold a significant share of household wealth. ScamSkeptic founder Matt Sanner joins 'America's Newsroom' to highlight how fraudsters utilize AI to mimic voices and create deepfakes. Sanner provides key strategies for families to identify these scams and protect their vulnerable loved ones.

The moving truck hasn't even left the driveway. Somewhere, a scammer may already know three things about you: your name, your new address and something about your age. Maybe not your exact age, but potentially enough information to make you a more attractive target.

Federal law sets specific rules for communities that qualify as housing for people 55 and older. One requirement says at least 80% of occupied units must house at least one person who is 55 or older. Those requirements come from the Housing for Older Persons Act.

That means an address inside a known 55+ community can give scammers and data brokers another clue about you. Once public records connect your name to that address, data brokers can add it to a much larger profile.

That is the part nobody mentions in the moving checklist. Here is how that profile can come together so quickly. More importantly, here is how you can reduce the personal information scammers can find.
FIVE DATA BROKER OPT-OUT MYTHS THAT LEAVE RETIREES EXPOSED
Scammers can combine property records, people-search listings and community information to build convincing profiles of new retirement community residents. (Getty Images)
Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the Protect Your Money replay

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, Protect Your Money From Today’s Biggest Threats, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay and download our financial protection checklist. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five simple ways to help defend yourself against AI scams, fraud, identity theft and financial hacks. You’ll learn how to set up bank alerts, strengthen your account logins, protect your phone number, freeze your credit and help secure your retirement savings against unauthorized transfers. No technical experience is needed.
Get the free replay and checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com
How moving to a 55+ community can expose your data
Moving into an age-restricted community does more than change your ZIP Code. It can quickly create a new, highly concentrated data profile.
Here's what can become available:

Your name and new address can appear in county property records after officials file the deed. Anyone can then search that information.Your HOA gets your contact information. Some communities also distribute resident directories with names, addresses and phone numbers.New-mover marketing companies identify people who recently relocated. They can then sell those details to advertisers.People-search sites such as Spokeo and Whitepages may update listings with your new address, age range and household details.Community Facebook groups, welcome committees and bulletin boards sometimes post new-neighbor introductions. Those posts may include names, photos or unit numbers.
Your name and new address can appear in county property records after officials file the deed. Anyone can then search that information.
Your HOA gets your contact information. Some communities also distribute resident directories with names, addresses and phone numbers.
New-mover marketing companies identify people who recently relocated. They can then sell those details to advertisers.
People-search sites such as Spokeo and Whitepages may update listings with your new address, age range and household details.
Community Facebook groups, welcome committees and bulletin boards sometimes post new-neighbor introductions. Those posts may include names, photos or unit numbers.
Each detail may seem harmless by itself. However, scammers can combine those details to build a convincing profile of you.
SELLING YOUR HOME? YOUR DATA IS ALREADY MOVING
Privacy experts recommend checking what information appears online, limiting community directory listings and requesting removal from data broker sites. (Getty Images)
Research shows scams can start soon after a move

Criminologists at Florida State University spent years studying financial exploitation inside a large Florida retirement community. Their findings should change how you think about your first few months in a new home. Residents told researchers that scammers targeted them immediately and repeatedly after they moved into the retirement community. They also faced scams far more often than before their move.

One of the study's authors, Julie Brancale, told AARP that residents faced targeting almost immediately after moving in. She said the attempts then continued. Her colleague, Thomas Blomberg, described another problem. People may move into gated communities expecting greater safety during retirement. Instead, they can face repeated scam attempts.

AARP's reporting on The Villages also highlights real cases of financial exploitation. The Villages is the country's largest 55+ community and has more than 150,000 residents. For example, a pair posing as pool contractors allegedly collected nearly $200,000 in down payments from six residents. Police later arrested them. A Leisure World resident in Maryland lost close to $800,000 in a gold-bar scam. Meanwhile, one local anti-fraud group estimates that it has recovered roughly $40 million for Florida victims over the years.
How retirement community scams can target your family

Here's the part that should get your attention. When a scammer searches for information about you, your adult children may appear too. Data broker profiles may list them as relatives and connect them to current addresses. As a result, a scam aimed at a new resident can spread to the whole family.

A criminal may never need to trick you directly. For example, someone could call your daughter and pretend to represent your new HOA. The caller could mention your real address and ask her to confirm a payment on your behalf. That request can sound convincing because the caller already knows personal details. The more information criminals collect beforehand, the easier they can make a fake story sound believable.
How big is fraud targeting older Americans?

This problem reaches far beyond individual retirement communities. The FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center logged more than 201,000 fraud complaints from Americans 60 and older in 2025. Those complaints totaled more than $7.7 billion in reported losses.

The FTC estimates that the true financial impact could reach as high as $81.5 billion after accounting for unreported cases. An analysis of FBI complaint data also found another troubling link. Roughly 72% of fraud categories affecting older adults can become more dangerous when attackers have access to personal information.
The takeaway is simple. Personal information gives scammers material they can use to make a fraudulent call, text or email sound more believable.
THE ONE THING SCAMMERS CHECK BEFORE TARGETING YOU ONLINE
Moving into a 55+ community can expose your age range, new address and family connections through public records and data broker sites. (iStock)
How to protect your privacy in a retirement community
You cannot prevent every county property record from becoming public. However, you can reduce how much additional information someone finds once they start looking.

First, ask your HOA or community manager whether you can limit or opt out of resident directory listings. Also, ask what information the community shares with other residents. If possible, remove your phone number, email address and photo from community directories.

Next, search your name, phone number and new address online to see what appears. People-search sites and data brokers may already connect your new location with your age range, relatives and previous addresses.
Remove your information from data broker sites

You can submit removal requests directly to people-search sites and data brokers that list your information, but doing it yourself can take a lot of time and effort. A data removal service can handle those requests on your behalf and continue checking whether your information reappears. Check out my top picks for data removal services and get a free scan to find out if your personal information is already out on the web by visiting CyberGuy.com.
Kurt's key takeaways

Moving into a 55+ community can create a privacy risk earlier than many people realize. What concerns me most is how quickly your new address can become connected to your age range, relatives and other personal details across public records and data broker sites.

The Florida State University research really stands out to me because residents reported scam attempts soon after moving. To me, that means privacy needs to be part of your moving checklist before you unpack the boxes, not something you think about after suspicious calls start coming in.

I would also pay close attention to what your information reveals about your family. Data broker profiles often connect relatives, previous addresses and household details. That gives scammers more ways to make a fake story sound convincing to you or someone close to you.

With Americans 60 and older reporting more than $7.7 billion in fraud losses to the FBI in 2025, I would not wait for a scam attempt to start protecting your information. Search for your name and address online, ask what your community shares and remove personal data from broker sites wherever possible.

title: Amazon drone delivery is coming to nearly 500 cities
summary: Amazon Prime Air drone delivery plans to reach nearly 500 U.S. cities by the end of 2026, but your yard and ZIP code may determine eligibility.
story: ‘The Five’ co-hosts discuss Amazon’s drone delivery service.

Amazon wants to make waiting for a package feel almost old-fashioned. Its Prime Air drone delivery service is gearing up for a major expansion, with plans to reach nearly 500 U.S. cities and towns by the end of 2026. For some shoppers, that could mean getting an eligible Amazon order dropped at home in as fast as 30 minutes.

That is a huge jump from where things stand today. Amazon currently operates Prime Air from 11 U.S. locations across 10 metro areas, and the company says its drones have already delivered hundreds of thousands of packages this year.

There is one detail worth keeping in mind when you hear that 500-city figure. Amazon is talking about communities served, rather than 500 individual drone hubs. Each Prime Air site can cover about 175 square miles, allowing one launch location to reach several nearby cities and towns.
So, could one of these drones soon be heading toward your neighborhood? Here's where Prime Air is available now, what it costs and what you should know before choosing drone delivery at checkout.
Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the Protect Your Money replay

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, Protect Your Money From Today’s Biggest Threats , has ended, but you can still watch the full replay and download our financial protection checklist. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five simple ways to help defend yourself against AI scams, fraud, identity theft and financial hacks. You’ll learn how to set up bank alerts, strengthen your account logins, protect your phone number, freeze your credit and help secure your retirement savings against unauthorized transfers. No technical experience is needed.
Get the free replay and checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com
DRONE DELIVERS 2 PIZZAS IN MINUTES
Amazon plans to expand Prime Air drone delivery to nearly 500 U.S. cities and towns by the end of 2026, with some orders arriving in as fast as 30 minutes. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
Where Amazon drone delivery works today

Prime Air currently serves the Phoenix, Tampa, Kansas City, Baton Rouge, Detroit, Omaha, Houston, Dallas, San Antonio and Waco metro areas. Those markets span seven states. Amazon says Chicago, Syracuse, Cleveland, Atlanta and Boise are next on its launch list. More communities are expected later this year.

If you live in one of those metro areas, that still does not guarantee a drone will appear as a delivery choice. Amazon says coverage can vary by ZIP code and address. When your home qualifies, the drone option appears while you shop or at checkout. That is the easiest way to know whether Prime Air has reached you. You do not need a separate app or a special Amazon account.
How fast can Amazon drone delivery reach your home?

Amazon advertises Prime Air delivery in as fast as 30 minutes. However, the company says most drone orders currently arrive around 60 minutes after checkout. That could still save you a trip when you need something quickly. If you need a charger before a trip or medicine you would rather not drive out for, an hour can feel very different from waiting until tomorrow.

Amazon says Prime Air can carry packages up to 5 pounds that fit roughly inside a large shoebox. The company says that makes more than 60% of the items customers buy most often eligible for drone delivery. The selection can include iPhones, Galaxy phones, AirPods, AirTags, Ring doorbells, groceries and household products. Of course, the exact selection depends on your location and what Amazon can safely load onto the drone.
UFC STAR CONOR MCGREGOR GOES VIRAL FOR DRONE DELIVERY FIASCO AFTER UNDERGOING KNEE SURGERY
Amazon’s Prime Air drones can carry eligible packages weighing up to 5 pounds, bringing select orders directly to customers’ homes. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
What Amazon drone delivery costs

What you pay for drone delivery depends on whether you have Prime and how much you order. Prime members pay no drone delivery fee when an eligible order totals $50 or more. Prime members pay $2.99 on smaller eligible orders. Customers without Prime pay $4.99.

That pricing could make drone delivery tempting when you need something quickly. On the other hand, paying a fee to shave a few hours off a routine purchase may feel unnecessary. The bigger question may be how quickly you begin treating one-hour delivery as normal once it becomes available.
How a Prime Air delivery reaches your yard

If Prime Air is available at your address, you will see the drone delivery option when you check out on Amazon. For your first order, you choose a delivery spot on your property. You can use that same spot again or change it later. When the drone arrives, it checks the area before releasing your package. Amazon says it looks for people, pets, vehicles and other obstacles that could get in the way.

That also means your yard could determine whether drone delivery works for you. Trees, landscaping or a pool may make it harder for the drone to find a safe place to drop your order. As Prime Air expands into more neighborhoods, Amazon will have to make sure each delivery spot gives the drone enough room to do its job safely.
What about safety, privacy and noise?

Amazon holds FAA Part 135 certification for Prime Air, the federal framework used for commercial drone package delivery. The FAA says Part 135 certification provides the path for operators carrying someone else's property for compensation beyond visual line of sight. Prime Air also uses a Detect-and-Avoid system. Amazon says the drone continuously scans the airspace around it and makes real-time decisions to avoid obstacles while flying.

Then there is the privacy question. Prime Air drones use onboard cameras and sensors for navigation. Amazon says the drones do not track individuals or record their movements. The company also says no person watches a live camera feed, because the drone processes the camera data onboard for navigation.

Noise may be the more noticeable issue for many neighborhoods. Amazon says the drone produces less sound during drop-off than an idling delivery truck parked at the curb. At cruising altitude, the company compares the sound with a window fan on low. Still, community complaints about drone noise have followed delivery programs before. As Amazon expands, local reaction could shape how smoothly Prime Air enters some neighborhoods.
Why the 500-city goal will be a major test

Amazon first showed off the idea of 30-minute drone delivery more than a decade ago. Since then, engineers have redesigned the aircraft while Amazon worked through aviation rules and local concerns. Now the company believes it has a version that can scale. Amazon CEO Andy Jassy told shareholders this year that Prime Air expects to reach communities with about 30 million customers by year-end. He also said the company plans to deliver half a billion packages by the end of the decade. Even with that ambition, drones will handle only a small slice of Amazon's overall deliveries for now. A drone carries one lightweight package at a time, while vans and trucks can move much larger loads.

Amazon also has plenty of competition. Walmart and Alphabet-owned Wing plan to expand drone delivery to more than 270 Walmart stores by 2027. Meanwhile, DoorDash has received FAA Part 135 certification for its own drone operation. The race has moved beyond proving that a drone can carry a package. Companies now have to show that people will use the service regularly and that neighborhoods will accept more aircraft overhead.
What this means to you

For most people, the first sign that Prime Air has reached their area will be simple: a drone delivery option shows up at checkout. If you need something quickly, that could be genuinely useful. A forgotten charger, medicine or another small item could arrive before you would normally make it to the store and back.

There are some limits to keep in mind. Your order has to fit Amazon's size and weight rules, your property needs a safe drop spot and bad weather can delay a flight. You may also have to decide how much speed is worth to you. More drone deliveries could mean more noise overhead and more questions about how these aircraft fit into everyday neighborhoods. If Prime Air becomes available at your address, I would try it when you actually need something fast. That is probably the best way to find out whether 30-minute delivery feels genuinely useful in your day-to-day life.
FIREWORKS ARE FADING, BUT THEIR HIGH-TECH REPLACEMENT COMES WITH NEW RISKS
Amazon says Prime Air drone delivery could reach communities serving about 30 million customers as the company rapidly expands the service. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
Kurt's key takeaways

Amazon has been chasing 30-minute drone delivery since Jeff Bezos introduced the idea in 2013. For years, it felt like a technology that was always coming soon. The scale of this new plan changes that conversation. I do not expect delivery vans to disappear. A 5-pound payload, changing weather, tricky yards and local rules give ground delivery plenty of work to do. But when you need a small item quickly, getting it in 30 to 60 minutes could become genuinely useful. What catches my attention most is how fast expectations can change. Same-day delivery once sounded incredibly fast. Now Amazon wants you thinking about whether an hour feels too long.

Would you welcome Amazon drones over your neighborhood if they could get an order to your home in under an hour, or would you rather keep those deliveries on the road? Let us know by writing to us at Cyberguy.com

title: Cybercrime losses near $21B: 5 ways to protect your money
summary: The FBI reports nearly $21 billion in cybercrime losses for 2025, up 26%, as AI scams make fake voices and identities more convincing than ever.
story: Cybercrime losses reached nearly $21 billion last year, prompting Kurt Knutsson to warn of increasingly sophisticated AI scams. He joins 'Fox & Friends Weekend' to break down the FBI data, highlighting that investment fraud alone cost victims $8.65 billion. Knutsson hosts a free live class to teach families how to protect their money and secure accounts.

Nearly $21 billion. That number jumped out at me when I looked at the FBI's latest cybercrime data. Behind that enormous loss are families who watched savings disappear and people who trusted the wrong investment pitch. Some victims had no clue someone was moving their money until they checked an account.

Americans reported nearly $21 billion in losses to cyber-enabled crime during 2025, up 26% from the year before. Investment fraud caused the biggest financial hit at about $8.65 billion. I recently joined "Fox & Friends Weekend" to talk about those numbers and a bigger problem I see coming. Scammers now have AI tools that can make a fake message, voice or identity far more believable than the clumsy scams many of us learned to recognize years ago. That changes how we need to protect our money.
Here are five practical steps you can take now to put stronger barriers between scammers and your savings.
Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the Protect Your Money replay

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, Protect Your Money From Today’s Biggest Threats , has ended, but you can still watch the full replay and download our financial protection checklist. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five simple ways to help defend yourself against AI scams, fraud, identity theft and financial hacks. You’ll learn how to set up bank alerts, strengthen your account logins, protect your phone number, freeze your credit and help secure your retirement savings against unauthorized transfers. No technical experience is needed.
Get the free replay and checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com
IDENTITY THEFT LOSSES SURGE 70% FOR OLDER AMERICANS

Americans reported nearly $21 billion in cyber-enabled crime losses in 2025, as scammers increasingly used artificial intelligence to make fraud more convincing. (Hollie Adams/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
AI is helping scammers sound more convincing

For years, one of the standard pieces of scam advice was to look for obvious mistakes. Maybe an email had terrible grammar. Perhaps the caller sounded suspicious. AI can now erase many of those clues.

The FBI says its Internet Crime Complaint Center received 22,364 complaints in 2025 that included AI-related information. Reported losses tied to those complaints reached about $893 million. The FBI also warns that criminals can use AI to create fake social profiles, cloned voices and convincing videos.

That gives scammers another way to build trust before asking for money or personal information. So telling you to "be careful" no longer feels like enough advice to me. I want barriers between a scammer and your money.
5 ways to protect your money from cybercrime
You cannot predict every scam that may come your way. However, you can put safeguards in place that make it harder for a criminal to reach your money.

Start with your bank and credit cards. Open the official app or website for each financial institution and look for notification settings. Turn on alerts for transactions and transfers. You may also be able to receive warnings about suspicious account activity.

The exact choices vary by bank. However, the goal stays simple. If money moves and you did not authorize it, you want to know quickly. I have talked with victims who discovered fraud long after criminals gained access. A real-time alert gives you a chance to call the financial institution and react much sooner.

Next, check the security settings on your bank, credit card and investment accounts. Use a strong password that you do not reuse elsewhere, which a password manager can help you create and store. Then turn on two-factor or multifactor authentication (2FA) wherever your financial institution offers it.

If the company supports an authenticator app, passkey or another stronger verification method, consider using that option. Texted security codes still add protection, although your phone number can become a target in a SIM swap attack.

Also protect the email account connected to your finances. A criminal who controls your email may be able to reset passwords or intercept account notifications. For a closer look at the different login options, see Are bank text codes enough to protect you?

Your phone number has quietly become part of your financial security. In a SIM swap or port-out scam, a criminal tricks a carrier into moving your number to another SIM or device. Once that happens, calls and texted security codes can start going to the scammer.

Contact your carrier or check its account-security settings. Look for a number transfer lock, port-out protection or another feature designed to block unauthorized transfers. If your phone suddenly loses service for no clear reason, pay attention. Contact your carrier from another device, especially if you also notice unusual activity involving your financial accounts.
IDENTITY RESTORATION: WHAT TO DO AFTER IDENTITY THEFT
Investment fraud accounted for about $8.65 billion in reported losses as cybercrime cost Americans nearly $21 billion in 2025. (Bildquelle/ullstein bild via Getty Images)

A credit freeze remains one of the strongest free tools available for preventing new-account fraud. You need to place a freeze separately with Equifax, Experian and TransUnion. Once active, the freeze restricts access to your credit file and makes it much harder for someone to open a new credit account using your identity.

A freeze does not hurt your credit score. You can also lift it when you legitimately need to apply for credit. One warning: go directly to the official credit bureau websites rather than clicking an ad or unfamiliar search result. Criminals know people search for credit-freeze help too. CyberGuy has step-by-step guidance on how to freeze your credit and clean up your online data at Cyberguy.com

This one worries me because retirement accounts can represent decades of someone's work. We recently covered a case involving a Colgate-Palmolive employee whose entire $751,430 401(k) was allegedly drained after an impostor changed the account's contact information. The case later settled on undisclosed terms.

Log in to your retirement and investment accounts and review their security settings. Make sure your contact information remains correct. Turn on account alerts and multifactor authentication. Then ask your brokerage or retirement-plan provider what protections it offers for withdrawals and transfers. Some providers offer additional verification or other controls that can make unauthorized transfers harder. This deserves the same attention you give your checking account. Maybe more.
Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay

If you want to go deeper than the steps above, I will walk through each one in more detail in my CyberGuy LIVE class, Protect Your Money From Today's Biggest Threats . The live event has ended, but the full replay and CyberGuy Money Protection checklist are available now.

In the class, I show you how to put these protections in place step by step, including where to look for bank alerts, how to strengthen account logins, ways to lock down your phone number, how to freeze your credit and what to ask your retirement or investment provider about added safeguards. You can pause the replay and work through each step at your own pace.
Watch the free CyberGuy LIVE replay and get the Money Protection checklist at CyberGuyLive.com
YOUR BANK MAY STOP TEXTING YOU SIX-DIGIT CODES
Artificial intelligence can help scammers create convincing messages, cloned voices, fake identities and videos designed to gain victims’ trust. (Nikos Pekiaridis/NurPhoto via Getty Images)
Kurt's key takeaways

What worries me about the FBI's nearly $21 billion figure goes beyond the size of the number. Scammers have become better at taking advantage of moments when people naturally trust what they see or hear. AI raises the stakes because a familiar voice or polished message can create a false sense of confidence. The FBI's numbers show how much money is already disappearing through cyber-enabled crime. I would rather see you build protections now than depend on spotting one tiny clue in the middle of a convincing scam. Turn on the alerts and secure the accounts holding your money. Then look at the protections surrounding your phone number, credit and retirement savings. Cybercriminals only need one good opportunity. Your job is to make that opportunity much harder to find.
