While there has been little recent movement on the front lines, the talks come ahead of what will likely be a difficult winter in Kyiv, which is facing a critical shortage of U.S.-made interceptor missiles able to repel Russian attacks on its energy infrastructure.

Sunday’s visit to Kyiv is believed to be the first to be made by Witkoff and Kushner, Trump’s son-in-law, as part of the peace effort. Witkoff has visited Moscow several times, most recently holding talks with Putin at the Kremlin in January.

Witkoff on Saturday appeared to strike a particularly warm tone during the meeting with Putin. In video published by Russia’s state-owned news outlet RIA Novosti, he told the Russian leader that the delegation had been reflecting on how “when we retire, we’ll have all these incredible stories and incredible memories, and yours will be right at the top of it all.”

Putin did not publicly signal any movement from his previous steep demands, which seek major concessions from Ukraine. He praised Witkoff and Kushner in the video, telling them: “I would like to say that working with you is a comfortable experience for us, and we certainly place a high level of trust in you throughout this process.”
Following the meeting Sunday with Zelenskyy, Witkoff also offered praise to the Ukrainian leader, saying his hospitality was “unsurpassed.”
A White House official said “substantive plans for the next steps” in the effort to end the war were at the center of the talks.
In a statement, the official said those next steps would be announced in the coming weeks, with the U.S. delegates looking forward to “equally productive meetings” in Ukraine.
They added that officials from the National Security Council, the State Department and the Treasury Department joined the meeting on Saturday, which lasted more than three hours.

Putin aide Yury Ushakov told Russian state media on Sunday that the meeting, which included an “informal setting at the dining table,” was “substantive, constructive, extremely frank and trusting,” noting it was the eighth time the U.S. delegation has visited Russia and that Putin had extended his “best wishes” to Trump.
In a nightly address on Friday, Zelenskyy said Kyiv’s goal was to have the “most constructive, substantive visit and negotiations possible with the American side.”
“We need to look for real options for how to bring this war to an end,” he said, adding: “We’ll see what proposals Steve and Jared have, and what they are told about this in Moscow.”
Pope Leo XIV said in remarks following his weekly Sunday Angelus prayer that he hoped the talks would “bear concrete fruit and open space for diplomacy.”

“My heart goes out to the suffering people, who for years have lived in anguish and fear,” he said, renewing his “appeal to put an end to the violence, to stop the destruction and to open hearts to dialogue and peace.”
Ahead of the talks, Russia had ramped up its attacks on Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities with relentless bombardments, exploiting Ukraine’s shortage of air defense systems.

A Russian drone on Friday hit one of the most important government buildings in Kyiv, the headquarters of Ukraine’s Security Service, known as the SBU, one of the agencies involved in the execution of deep-strike operations inside Russia.
In a social media post Saturday, Zelenskyy said Russia had launched overnight strikes on Kyiv and Boryspil international airports, linking the attack to the U.S. visit.
“Clearly, these Russian strikes on the airports are a reaction to the discussions and preparations for the possibility of the U.S. side using an aircraft to travel to Ukraine,” he said.
He said Kyiv had “taken note of this Russian move” and would “adjust our operation accordingly regarding Russian airspace, which has become dangerous because of our drones and missiles in the sky.”

Speaking with reporters on Friday during an event in the Oval Office, Trump said Kushner and Witkoff had been doing a “great job” in their efforts on the peace process ahead of their visits to Moscow and Kyiv.
“We sent them over to see whether or not we can get something done,” he said. “And there may be a good chance that we’ll do it.”

title: U.S. strikes 3 Iranian oil tankers after Iran targets Navy warships, military says
summary: U.S. Central Command said no American personnel were harmed in the Iranian missile attacks.
story: U.S. forces struck three Iranian oil tankers Saturday after Iran launched ballistic missiles toward two U.S. Navy ships, the U.S. military said.
A U.S. aircraft carrier and guided missile destroyer evaded multiple attacks by Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, U.S. Central Command said in a statement. No American personnel were harmed.

CENTCOM said U.S. forces retaliated by permanently disabling two crude oil carriers, the M/T Downy off the coast of Kharg Island and the M/T Stark 1 near Jask. Forces also destroyed a third vessel, the M/T Kylo near the Gulf of Oman.
The Kylo was not carrying oil at the time and its crew was directed to abandon the vessel before American forces struck it in multiple locations, CENTCOM said.

“If you shoot at two of our ships, we will impose an even higher economic cost — taking out three of yours,” Adm. Brad Cooper, the commander of CENTCOM, said in a statement. “We will not hesitate to defend American forces, and if necessary, destroy Iran’s limited and exposed oil fleet.”
Iran’s Foreign Ministry strongly condemned the U.S. strikes, calling them “illegal and aggressive” and accusing Washington of waging a naval blockade and economic war against Iran.

In a statement carried by Iranian state media IRIB, the ministry said the attacks violated the United Nations Charter and constituted a war crime and a threat to international peace and commercial shipping.

Iranian semiofficial news agency Fars reported that the IRGC attacked with ballistic missiles an aircraft carrier and a military destroyer that had been taking part in the naval blockade and “harassing Iranian vessels.”
On Sunday, the IRGC also said it struck an unmanned U.S. vessel trying to enter the Strait of Hormuz. The U.S. did not immediately confirm the purported attack.

Kharg Island, a tiny but strategic island 15 miles off the coast of Iran in the Persian Gulf, plays a central role in the country’s oil industry. There are also military capabilities there, including air defenses and mines buried underground.

The site has repeatedly emerged as a flashpoint during the conflict. U.S. forces struck military targets on the island in March but deliberately spared its oil infrastructure. President Donald Trump said at the time that the U.S. could target the energy facilities if Iran continued interfering with shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.

The island is critical to Iran’s finances. Petras Katinas, a research fellow at the Royal United Services Institute, previously told NBC News that Kharg is the “backbone” of Iran’s oil trade infrastructure and the primary gateway for the country’s oil reserves.

Iranian media reported earlier Saturday that a tanker near Kharg had been hit by U.S. missiles and that its crew was being evacuated. No casualties were reported, according to Iran’s semiofficial Tasnim news agency.

title: Serbia accused of ‘glorifying’ convicted war criminal Ratko Mladić ahead of funeral
summary: BELGRADE, Serbia — The European Union’s Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos on Friday canceled an upcoming visit to candidate nation Serbia over what she described as the “glorification” of former Bosnian Serb army commander Ratko Mladić following his death.
story: BELGRADE, Serbia — The European Union’s Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos on Friday canceled an upcoming visit to candidate nation Serbia over what she described as the “glorification” of former Bosnian Serb army commander Ratko Mladić following his death. Mladić was convicted of genocide by a U.N. court but remains a hero to many Serbs.
Mladić’s remains were flown to Belgrade on a Serbian government plane from The Hague, Netherlands, on Thursday, a week after his death and days ahead of his burial in a Belgrade cemetery.

Mladić was sentenced in 2017 to life imprisonment for orchestrating the massacre of more than 8,000 Muslims in Srebrenica in 1995; the yearslong siege of the Bosnian capital of Sarajevo during the 1992-95 conflict; and other war crimes, including setting up concentration camps for detained non-Serb civilians and enemy soldiers.

Upon landing in Belgrade, Mladić’s coffin was wrapped in the national flag and Serbian soldiers carried his body to a van for transport to the military hospital. Serbia’s Justice Minister Nenad Vujic was on the plane with Mladić’s family members and nationalist admirers lit flares as the convoy passed.
Kos said on X that “the glorification surrounding his death is incompatible with the values on which the EU path is built.”
“Ratko Mladić was convicted of genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes,” Kos said. “The return of his remains to Belgrade reminds Europe of the darkest pages in our recent history.”

In Belgrade, regional N1 television quoted Serbia’s populist President Aleksandar Vučić as saying that Kos’s explanation was “very short but stupid.” Vučić said Kos did not specify “who glorified anything” but that “I guess we should ban people from showing up, ban the funeral.”
Earlier Friday, Kos said the next days “will be a very important test” for Serbia ahead of the burial, which could draw thousands of admirers.
Mladić to be buried Monday in Belgrade

Mladić’s son, Darko Mladić, said at a news conference Friday that a military commemoration is planned for Saturday. Mladić’s coffin will be placed in a church in Belgrade on Monday morning so people can pay their respects before his funeral and burial later that day.

Vučić had previously said Mladić would be buried with full state honors, sparking outrage across the Balkans, where ethnic divisions persist decades after the 1992-95 war in Bosnia killed over 100,000 people and displaced millions.
Last year, Serbia buried another convicted war criminal, the former army chief of staff Nebojša Pavković, with full military honors at a cemetery for distinguished individuals.

Serbia, which backed Bosnian Serb forces during the war, is formally seeking EU membership but remains defiant over its war role, accusing the West of anti-Serb bias. After Mladić died last week, thousands of Serbs in their political entity in Bosnia and many in Serbia held vigils in his honor. Thousands could attend the funeral.
Other European officials condemn Mladić glorification

The Council of Europe Commissioner for Human Rights, Michael O’Flaherty, on Friday urged authorities in Serbia and in the Serb-run entity of Bosnia to “counter the glorification of convicted war criminals,” which is illegal in Bosnia and “is not protected speech under the European Convention on Human Rights.”
“I abhor the public glorification of Ratko Mladić, a deceased war criminal convicted for the Srebrenica genocide and crimes against humanity,” O’Flaherty said in a statement.

Belgium’s Foreign Minister Maxime Prevot said granting funeral honors for Mladić would be “shameful and disrespectful for the victims,” adding: “I condemn that act in the strongest terms, and have passed this message to my Serbian counterpart in charge of European affairs this morning.”

Calls are also multiplying for Europe’s biggest political bloc - the European People’s Party - to cut its ties to Vučić’s Serbian Progressive Party. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen is a member of the EPP, along with European Parliament President Roberta Metsola and other top officials.

Vladimir Prebilic, a European Parliament member from Slovenia, urged the EPP to “stop acting as a safe haven” for Vučić’s party, which he said “openly celebrates convicted war criminals and rolls out the red carpet for the ‘Butcher of Bosnia.”’
Serbia’s president says he has meetings on Monday

In Serbia, Vučić, who is a former extreme nationalist who backed Serbia’s expansionist policies in the past, said Friday that he has previously scheduled meetings Monday, and the funeral arrangements were made by Mladić’s family.
“I have spoken to the Mladić family and I wish it all passes in a dignified way,” Vučić said, according to the pro-government Informer television.
“I did all I could so that the funeral would pass as it should,” he added without elaborating.
Serbia’s EU bid has stalled due to democratic backsliding and Vučić’s refusal to join international sanctions against Russia over the invasion of Ukraine.

The massacre in Srebrenica was Europe’s first acknowledged genocide after World War II. A U.N. “safe haven” for Bosniaks (Bosnian Muslims), Srebrenica ended up being overrun by Serbs who forced men and boys to strip, killed them and bulldozed their bodies into mass graves.
Mladić was one of the most notorious figures of the war in Bosnia that left more than 100,000 people dead and over 1 million homeless before it ended in 1995 in a U.S.-brokered peace agreement.

title: Two trapped workers pulled alive from Nepal tunnel more than a week after deadly floods
summary: Two workers in Nepal were pulled out alive from a hydropower tunnel on Friday, some nine days after devastating floods swept the Himalayan region and left thousands of people missing.
story: POKHARA, Nepal — Two workers in Nepal were pulled out alive from a hydropower tunnel Friday, nine days after devastating floods swept the Himalayan region and left thousands of people dead or missing.

In a rare glimmer of hope, emergency teams rescued two men —  a mechanical foreman named Sanjay Sah, 30, and a mechanical supervisor named Kabir Maharjan, 45, according to Nepal’s army and the country’s National Disaster Risk Reduction & Management Authority. A body was also recovered, Nepal’s army said.
Two Nepal flood survivors rescued from hydropower tunnel

Rescue officials said the voices of other workers could be heard inside the tunnel at the Trishuli 3A hydropower plant along the Trishuli River in Nepal’s border district of Rasuwa. At least 557 workers are still believed to be missing there, with about 115 believed to be trapped in the main tunnel, according to the Independent Power Producers Association of Nepal.
In a video shared by Nepalese authorities, Sah said he spent his days trapped underground “chanting mantras to give myself hope” while hearing others trapped and calling out for help.
Sah said the “primary duty” of his job is “to safeguard everyone’s life,” adding that there were some 40 to 50 people in the tunnel at the time of the incident.
“I made sure to evacuate everyone else, but I didn’t get the chance to escape myself,” he said, speaking from the hospital in the video.
He said there could still be other survivors on his side of the tunnel, while there could be workers on the powerhouse side of the tunnel “who didn’t make it out in time.”

Nepal’s army released images of the dramatic rescue on its official Facebook page, including one showing the first rescued worker covered in mud and being carried from the site on a rescuer’s shoulder.
“When hope is alive, even the impossible becomes possible,” the image caption read.
Officials said both men were flown to a hospital in Kathmandu, the capital, for treatment.

“I can’t explain what we are feeling at the moment. We are just grateful to God,” Amir Maharjan, the brother of one of the rescued workers, told The Associated Press. He said the family was on its way to the hospital to see him.
The large-scale operation has involved 75 army personnel, 18 police officers and multiple experts, the army said.
Army spokesperson Brig. Gen. Raja Ram Basnet said one of the survivors told rescuers that more people were still alive inside the tunnel.
“We are waiting for the rescue of more and more people,” Communication Minister Bikram Timilsina wrote on his Facebook page.
More than 900 workers are missing from about a dozen hydropower projects in Nepal, with roughly 500 believed to be trapped in tunnels, according to local officials.

Rescuers have been struggling to access the hydropower projects, many of which are in remote, mountainous areas, with bad weather adding to the difficulties. The flooding damaged roads and collapsed sections of tunnels, filling them with mud and other debris and blocking some entrances.

Aided by foreign experts, rescue teams have been working around the clock using controlled blasts, excavators and earth-moving equipment to try to reach the trapped workers amid concerns about air quality in the tunnels and the workers’ access to drinking water.
Nepal’s army said Friday that a separate rescue effort had recovered two bodies from a tunnel at the Langtang Hydropower Project.

Authorities in Nepal say at least 1,294 people were killed and more than 5,000 remain missing after the Aug. 26 disaster, which is believed to have been set off by a high-altitude glacier collapse on the border between Nepal and China’s Tibet region.
Nepal’s disaster agency estimated Friday that flooding caused at least 387.5 billion Nepalese rupees ($2.5 billion) in damage to infrastructure and property.

Nepalese authorities said a national day of mourning will be observed on Sept. 7 in honor of those who lost their lives during the flood. The national flag will be flown at half-staff at government offices and Nepali embassies and missions abroad.

Rescue efforts are also still underway in China, where a mudslide hit a major land crossing between the two countries, with the only road to the site in Tibet’s Gyirong county fully reopening only Wednesday. Chinese officials say at least 31 people were killed and 531 are missing on the Tibet side of the border.

More than 800 foreign nationals are among those missing in the area, which is popular with trekkers and pilgrims. According to the State Department, 75 Americans remained unaccounted for as of Wednesday, while 16 had made their way to safety.
Sunil Pandey reported from Pokhara, Nepal, and Adela Suliman from London.

title: Senior aides to British Trump ally Nigel Farage step down after foreign funding sting
summary: Britain’s populist Reform UK said two senior aides to leader Nigel Farage stepped down on Friday after an undercover investigation alleged the party had broken electoral law by arranging for a foreign donor to pay for political polling.
story: Britain’s populist Reform UK said two senior aides to leader Nigel Farage stepped down on Friday after an undercover investigation alleged the party had broken electoral law by arranging for a foreign donor to pay for political polling.
Reform denied any wrongdoing and said it had been the victim of a hoax perpetrated by ⁠climate activists.
The governing Labour Party wrote to the police asking them to investigate possible criminal offences, including an alleged proposal to channel a larger overseas donation through a UK intermediary.

The investigation, broadcast by public British broadcaster Channel 4 just as Reform’s annual conference opened to the public, said two senior figures in Reform had arranged for a U.S. company to pay more than £30,000 ($40,000) for three opinion polls commissioned by the party.
Such an arrangement could breach British laws on political funding, which ⁠ban foreign donations.

Posing as wealthy donors from the United States with British connections, the ​undercover ⁠team from an investigative group called Verbatim said it spent a year speaking to top officials in Reform about possible donations, culminating in a lunch with Farage.

Channel 4 said Verbatim was an independent organisation founded by journalists from the Centre for Climate Reporting, but that it ⁠had verified their findings, which included covertly filmed footage of meetings.

Farage, a Trump ally and former Brexit campaigner who is under parliamentary investigation over earlier donations, ​told LBC radio: “The party ⁠has broken no laws. The party has not taken any ‌dodgy money or anything like that whatsoever.”
Party’s poll lead has faltered

Reform, which has seen its commanding lead in opinion polls falter over undeclared donor allegations, announced an internal investigation and said the two officials featured in the undercover filming — head of policy James Orr and Farage’s right-hand man Dan ‌Jukes — had stepped down pending its results.
Orr, a philosophy professor at the University of ‌Cambridge and friend of U.S. Vice President JD Vance, said in a video on X that Reform had not been involved in commissioning the poll.
“There’s absolutely no way this could amount to a benefit or donation in kind at all,” he said.

“It wasn’t internal party polling. It wasn’t Reform UK’s poll. It was a public poll arranged by an independent person paying an ⁠independent pollster, and those polls were published immediately for the general public.”
The latest accusations over donations come on the first public day of the party’s annual conference, which Farage had hoped would offer him a chance of a reset after a difficult summer.

Farage, 62, is being investigated by a parliamentary watchdog over a £5 million donation from crypto-billionaire Christopher Harborne in 2024. He denies any wrongdoing but has seen support for his party soften in recent weeks.
Labour allege further possible breaches

On Friday, Farage said both Jukes and Orr had “said things that shouldn’t have been said” in relation to donations purportedly originating in the United States, but no such donation had been accepted by the party and that the two had been “entrapped”.

In a letter to the Metropolitan Police, Labour said ‌the documentary contained two further possible breaches: discussion of channelling a donation from a U.S.-based donor through a UK-based son and the suggestion ​that similar methods have been used in the past.
A spokesperson for Reform said: “Reform UK has been the target of a hoax ‌perpetrated by foreign-funded, climate change activists posing as would-be party donors. The ⁠party denies any wrongdoing.
“Reform UK has a robust vetting process for prospective donors approved by the Electoral Commission.”
The Metropolitan Police said ⁠it was aware of the allegations in the broadcast and would assess any information provided to them. This did not amount to the formal launch of an investigation.

The Electoral Commission, which oversees ‌and regulates political finance in Britain, said: “We are ​considering all relevant information, in line with our regulatory remit, and we are ‌in touch with the Met Police.
“The Electoral Commission has not ​approved the donor vetting process for Reform, or any other party. Parties are responsible for ensuring their internal processes and controls are fit for purpose.”

title: In Nepal, mourners hold symbolic cremation for missing loved ones
summary: As hopes for those still missing fade, families without the remains of their relatives are burning effigies on miniature funeral pyres.
story: The wall of ice, water and rock that tore through Nepal last week has claimed more than 1,200 lives and left more than 4,000 missing, depriving many grieving families of a basic rite: funerals.

The scale of the disaster has proved challenging for authorities, with morgues overwhelmed by a large number of unidentified remains. In many cases, bodies have been washed far downstream and rendered unrecognizable, while others still missing are feared to have been buried in the torrent of thick mud.
As hopes fade that survivors will be found, a week on from the disaster, family members without the remains of their loved ones have begun to hold symbolic cremations.
The ceremonies provide an outlet for the grief and uncertainty that have gripped so many in Nepal, and ensure that a key religious rite is afforded to the dead.

At Kathmandu’s Pashupatinath Temple, the most revered Hindu temple in Nepal, mourners gathered Wednesday to mark the loss of missing loved ones. On the banks of the holy Bagmati River, they burned effigies made of kusa grass, also called darbha, a plant used in Hindu rituals, on miniature funeral pyres.
The small stick figures, wrapped in orange cloth, were rubbed in paste and covered in garlands of orange flowers.
